# Disclosure

A button that shows and hides a panel of content, expanded in place.

```tsx
import { Disclosure } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `disclosure` |
| Family | content |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | `state-layer`, `icon` |

## Behavior

A trigger that shows and hides a panel, built on `getDisclosureProps` — the primitive three navigation components already use. Open state is controlled or uncontrolled; Escape closes it from either half and hands focus back to the trigger.

- **This is a disclosure and not a menu, and the difference is the whole reason the primitive exists separately** — A menu promises a keyboard model — one tab stop, arrow keys, typeahead — that assistive technology announces and users then expect. A disclosure promises nothing beyond "this button reveals that", and everything inside the panel stays in the tab order where it was. Reaching for `role="menu"` on a panel of links or form fields is among the commonest mistakes in this area, and `getDisclosureProps` documents it at length. This component is the standalone consumer of that argument.
- **Closed empties the panel rather than removing it** — Two promises pull against each other here and the split keeps both. The content is unmounted, for the reason `SideNav` first gave: hidden content is still reachable by find-in-page, so a panel claiming to be collapsed could be scrolled to and read, and a chart inside a closed section would go on measuring a hidden box. But the panel ELEMENT stays, empty and `hidden`, because `getDisclosureProps` points `aria-controls` at it whether open or shut — a reference that appears and disappears is one assistive technology has to re-read to discover, and a dangling IDREF is simply ignored, which made that reference inert exactly half the time. An empty hidden shell is reachable by no find-in-page and resolves for every reader. The cost is unchanged: state inside the panel resets, which is the caller's to manage and is stated in `children`'s entry.
- **It does not animate open in this version** — Transitioning to `height: auto` needs either a measured pixel height or a `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr` wrapper, and both put a second element around the caller's content purely to move it. Unmounting when closed forecloses the transition anyway — there is nothing in the DOM to animate from. The chevron rotates, which is the part that reports the state change, and the panel appears. Animating the panel is its own pass with its own decision about the wrapper.
- **`headingLevel` is optional and there is no default** — The APG's disclosure pattern is a bare button, and that is right for one "Show advanced options" in a form. The APG's accordion pattern wraps each trigger in a heading, and that is what makes a stack of sections navigable by heading. Those are the same component in two situations, so the wrapper is a prop rather than a second component — and it has no default for the reason `Heading`'s `level` has none: only the caller knows the depth, and a component that guessed would produce a page of `h3`s.
- **It owns no box, no background and no rule between sections** — A lone disclosure sits in running content, where a border and a padded box would be an uninvited card. The rules that divide a stack of sections are a property of the stack — they need to know which section is first and last — and inventing them here would mean every standalone use has to override them. Same reasoning as `Heading` carrying no margin.
- **An accordion — a set where opening one closes the others — is a different entry, and this is not it** — That behavior needs an owner above the individual sections: something holding which one is open, the way `RadioGroup` holds the selected radio and `ToggleButtonGroup` holds its selection mode. A `single`/`multiple` prop on the unit could not express it, because a unit cannot close its siblings. `accordion` resolves here for now because one collapsible section is what most people asking for one actually want; when the coordinating entry ships, the alias moves to it.
- **`disabled` is `aria-disabled`, and the primitive blocks the activation** — This system's rule for every interactive primitive: a disabled control stays focusable and screen-reader-discoverable, and `getDisclosureProps` already guards the click and emits `aria-disabled` rather than the native attribute. Nothing new is decided here — it is named so the contract does not read as though the question were open.
- **Escape closes it from the trigger as well as from inside the panel** — A disclosure does not move focus when it opens, so after the trigger is pressed focus is still on the trigger. An Escape handler bound only to the panel would therefore never fire in the commonest case: open it, press Escape, nothing happens. The primitive puts the same handler on both halves for exactly this, and leaves the key alone while closed so a surrounding Dialog still receives it.

## Props

Extends `Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "title" | "children">`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | The trigger's label — what the button says it will reveal. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The content the trigger reveals. |
| `headingLevel?` | `DisclosureHeadingLevel` | — | Wraps the trigger in a heading at this level, turning a stack of these into an accordion someone can navigate by heading. |
| `open?` | `boolean` | — | Controls the panel from outside, for when something other than the trigger decides. |
| `defaultOpen?` | `boolean` | `false` | The starting state when the component owns it. |
| `onOpenChange?` | `(open: boolean) => void` | — | Fires when the trigger is pressed or Escape closes the panel. |
| `disabled?` | `boolean` | `false` | Marks the disclosure unavailable without removing it from the page. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it. |

### `title`

```ts
title: ReactNode
```

The trigger's label — what the button says it will reveal.

**Use when**

- A short phrase naming the content, not the action: "Shipping address", not "Show shipping address". The button already announces that it expands.

**Don't use for**

- A sentence. The trigger is a control at control size, and a label that wraps has stopped being one.
- Anything interactive. A button inside a button does not nest, and the browser will not render what you wrote.

**Accessibility** Becomes the trigger's accessible name, and — through `aria-labelledby` — the panel's as well, so the revealed region is never anonymous. With `headingLevel` set it is also the heading's text.

### `children`

```ts
children: ReactNode
```

The content the trigger reveals.

**Use when**

- Anything: prose, a form, a table. The panel is a plain region and imposes no structure on it.

**Don't use for**

- Content that must keep state while closed. The panel's content unmounts rather than hiding, so a half-filled form inside it is gone on reopen — lift that state above the disclosure.

**Accessibility** Everything inside stays in the tab order exactly where it is. That is the promise a disclosure makes and a menu does not.

### `headingLevel`

```ts
headingLevel?: DisclosureHeadingLevel
```

Wraps the trigger in a heading at this level, turning a stack of these into an accordion someone can navigate by heading.

Source doc: Wraps the trigger in a heading at this level, so a stack of these is navigable by heading.

**Use when**

- On every section of a set that divides a page — the level below whatever heading the set sits under.
- Left off for a single disclosure inside a form or a paragraph, which heads nothing.

**Don't use for**

- Picking it for size. The trigger is a control and takes the control type scale at every level; this only changes what the outline says.

**Accessibility** The APG's accordion pattern is a heading containing a button, and that pairing is what lets a reader jump between sections instead of tabbing through them. A skipped level breaks that navigation, which is why there is no default — only the caller knows the depth.

### `open`

```ts
open?: boolean
```

Controls the panel from outside, for when something other than the trigger decides.

**Use when**

- Opening the section that holds a failed field after a form is submitted.
- Persisting which sections a reader had open across a navigation.

**Don't use for**

- Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`. One of them owns the state; passing both means the uncontrolled value is silently ignored from the first render.

**Conflicts with** `defaultOpen`

**Accessibility** Drives `aria-expanded` on the trigger. Because the panel unmounts when closed, this prop is also what decides whether its content exists at all.

### `defaultOpen`

```ts
defaultOpen?: boolean = false
```

The starting state when the component owns it.

**Use when**

- Opening the one section that is the point of the page, leaving the rest closed.
- Opening the section containing the current item, the way `SideNav` expands the group holding the current page — a reader inside a collapsed group cannot see where they are.

**Don't use for**

- Opening everything. A set that starts fully open is a page with headings in it, and the disclosures are only costing the reader a click to get back to.

**Conflicts with** `open`

### `onOpenChange`

```ts
onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void
```

Fires when the trigger is pressed or Escape closes the panel.

**Use when**

- Storing which sections a reader keeps open.
- Loading the section's content the first time it opens.

**Don't use for**

- Treating it as a click handler. Escape calls it too, and so does any future way of closing the panel.

**Accessibility** The component returns focus to the trigger when Escape closes the panel, before this fires — a caller does not have to restore it and should not fight it.

### `disabled`

```ts
disabled?: boolean = false
```

Marks the disclosure unavailable without removing it from the page.

**Use when**

- A section that has nothing in it yet, where hiding it entirely would make the page change shape.

**Don't use for**

- Hiding content the reader is not allowed to see. Disabled is a statement about the control, not a security boundary, and the panel's absence is not enforcement.

**Accessibility** `aria-disabled`, never the native attribute: the trigger stays focusable and discoverable, and the primitive blocks the activation. Styled with state.disabled-opacity.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.

**Use when**

- The margin the page wants around it, or the rule between it and the next one, neither of which this component owns.

**Don't use for**

- Rebuilding the trigger's hover. Compose `.rata-state-layer`, which it already carries.

## Use cases

### One optional section in a form

Settings most people never change, kept off the page until asked for.

```tsx
<Disclosure title="Advanced options">
  <TextField label="Retry limit" />
</Disclosure>
```

No `headingLevel`: this heads nothing and nobody navigates to it. The fields inside stay in the tab order where they are, which is the promise that makes a disclosure the right pattern here rather than a menu.

### A page divided into sections

Several disclosures in a row, each a part of one document.

```tsx
<Disclosure title="Shipping address" headingLevel={3} defaultOpen>
  <Text>Where the order goes.</Text>
</Disclosure>
```

`headingLevel` is what makes the set navigable by heading instead of only by tabbing. Level 3 because the section it sits in is headed by an h2 — the same outline rule `Heading` enforces.

### Opened from outside by something that went wrong

A submit failed and the offending field is inside a collapsed section.

```tsx
<Disclosure title="Billing" open={hasBillingError} onOpenChange={setBillingOpen}>
  <TextField label="Card number" status="invalid" message="Check this number." />
</Disclosure>
```

Controlled, because the trigger is no longer the only thing that decides. A reader must never be shown an error message about a field they cannot see.

### Reaching for the wrong component

The panel holds commands rather than content — Rename, Duplicate, Delete.

```tsx
<Disclosure title="Actions">
  <Button variant="tertiary">Rename</Button>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Delete</Button>
</Disclosure>
```

Don't. That is `Menu`: a list of commands promises arrow-key navigation and one tab stop, and a disclosure gives neither — so every command lands in the page's tab order. The two are different ARIA patterns for different things, which is exactly why the primitive is separate from `getMenuProps`.

## Real usage in this repo

```tsx
<Disclosure title="Advanced options">
          <TextField label="Retry limit" description="How many times to try again." />
        </Disclosure>
```

## Token recipe

### base

Nothing. The component owns no box, no background and no rule — a lone disclosure sits in running content, and the divider between stacked sections belongs to the set rather than to the unit.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| box | `none — see the decision on why the rules between sections are not this component's` |

### trigger

A control, sized and padded from the control scale so it lines up with the buttons around it. Full-bleed in its inline axis: the whole row is the target, which is what makes a wide section header feel pressable rather than only its text.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| min-block-size | `size.control.md as a FLOOR rather than a fixed height — a section title long enough to wrap must be allowed to, the same call `SideNav` made for its rows. A fixed block-size would clip the second line.` |
| padding-inline | `space.control.padding-inline.sm` |
| border-radius | `radius.element` |
| colour | `theme.fg.primary` |
| font-size | `type.control.size.md` |
| font-weight | `type.control.weight` |
| gap between the label and the chevron | `space.gap.sm` |
| chevron size | `size.icon.text` |
| hover / press | `compose the .rata-state-layer class` |
| focus ring | `theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible` |
| disabled | `state.disabled-opacity` |

### chevron

The only thing that moves. It rotates between the two states at the interactive duration, which is the pair reserved for a control answering a press.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| transition | `motion.interactive.duration with motion.interactive.easing` |
| colour | `currentColor — it repeats what aria-expanded already says, so it can never disagree with the trigger it sits in` |

### panel

The revealed content. Indented to the trigger's own inline padding so the two read as one block, and given room above it rather than below — what follows the disclosure is the page's spacing problem, not this component's.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| padding-block-start | `space.padding.sm` |
| padding-inline | `space.control.padding-inline.sm — matching the trigger, so the label and the content it reveals share an edge` |
| colour | `inherited — the panel holds whatever the caller puts in it and tints none of it` |
| when closed | `display: none via [hidden] — stated rather than left to the UA stylesheet, because a `display` added to this rule later would silently outrank it and start painting an empty box` |
